newsitem.title: UK: UK rail sell-off nears final stop with NWRR deal.
newsitem.headline: UK rail sell-off nears final stop with NWRR deal.

text.p: The controversial privatisation of Britain's railway network neared its final stop this week after authorities awarded the North West Regional Railways (NWRR) franchise to Great Western Holdings Ltd.

Of the 25 franchises carved out of British Rail's post-war monopoly, only three franchises for routes in central England, Scotland and the western main line from London to Scotland, now remain open to private bids before the election, due by May 22.

The Office of Passenger Rail Franchising (Opraf) said late on Tuesday that Great Western -- a consortium of management and employees, bus and train operator FirstBus Plc and the 3i venture capital firm -- had won the franchise.
On Wednesday, Opraf said Great Western had pledged to pump 1.5 million pounds into the seven-year franchise to refurbish trains and five million to improve stations.
The company would also buy 70 new diesel trains by March 2000 and invest one million pounds a year on security.
The NWRR franchise covers local and regional passenger rail services in north western England and north Wales as well as urban services around Manchester and Liverpool.

Under the terms of the agreement, Great Western would operate at least the current number of train miles and add to services, including routes between Liverpool and Manchester and between Manchester and Wigan or Preston, Opraf said.
In return, Great Western would receive national and local government subsidies averaging 148.3 million pounds ($238 million) a year over the full term of the franchise, Opraf said.

"Today's announcement is excellent news for passengers in the north west who can now look forward to improved services...and improved rolling stock," Opraf's franchising director John O'Brien said in a statement.
Transport secretary George Young called the franchise award a milestone in the privatisation programme and "an excellent deal for passengers and taxpayers."
The award marks Great Western's second franchise -- the consortium was created when it won one of the first train operating companies, Great Western Rail last year.
It is also the latest foray into railways by bus operators, who have sought to take advantage of the transport privatisation programme driven on by John Major's Conservative government.

Another FirstBus venture, Straightforward Lines Ltd, is one of two finalists competing for the Central Trains franchise. Central, based in Birmingham, operates services in central England and extending in Wales and East Anglia. FirstBus's rival on the shortlist is another rail and bus operator, National Express Group Plc, Opraf said last week.
Only the ScotRail and Intercity West Coast franchises would be left once Central Trains is awarded. Preferred bidders have been named for all Britain's other franchises.
FirstBus shares were down 1-1/2p at 234-1/2 in London although transport stocks have soared in the past year.
Dealers noted the franchise award had been widely expected after the Great Western consortium was named as preferred bidder for North West Regional Railways a week ago. ($1=.6237 Pound)
